prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- More than one million people in Darfur are at risk of losing food, water and shelter in coming months, following the expulsion of international aid groups by Sudan's government, the United Nations' chief humanitarian coordinator said Tuesday. A Doctors without Borders medic helps a sick child in a Darfur refugee camp. The statement by coordinator John Holmes comes after a joint U.N.-Sudanese assessment of the situation. The information was gathered from March 11-18 in hopes of stemming further troubles in Darfur after Sudan's government expelled 13 international relief organizations from the wartorn region. The announcement came on the same day that President Omar al-Bashir, now an indicted war criminal, ignored the threat of arrest by traveling abroad to Eritrea. Also Tuesday, a Sudanese staffer working for a Canadian relief group was shot dead in Darfur. A full report of the assessment will be released soon, according to the U.N., but an executive summary and recommendations were made available on Tuesday. "While a significant effort is being made by the government, by the U.N., by the NGOs [nongovernmental organizations] which are left, to plug some of the immediate gaps in these areas, these are at the same time, 'Band-Aid' solutions, not long term solutions," Holmes said. The U.N. estimates that 1.5 million people in Darfur are dependent on healthcare support, 1.1 million need regular food aid, and another 1 million are in need of clean drinking water. The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which is still allowed to operate in Sudan, is carrying out a one-time-only distribution program in March and April, but that new partners will be needed to continue delivering food after April. After the International Criminal Court charged Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity on March 4, Khartoum expelled 13 international aid agencies and revoked the permits of three organizations in the country. Bashir -- the first sitting head of state to be charged with war crimes by the court -- has continued to say that humanitarian efforts in the country should be "Sudanized." "Within a year, we don't want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen," he said at a rally a week after his arrest warrant was issued. Holmes said that 13,000 to 14,000 aid workers in the region already were Sudanese nationals. Holmes said the cooperation and technical help from the Sudanese government on the assessment was a good step forward. But he called it "only the first of many steps if the people in Darfur are not going to suffer major consequences from these expulsions." Sudan's U.N. Ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly said he has information implicating the ousted organizations in activities contrary to their humanitarian missions. He has yet to make any of that information public. One claim is that some organizations acted as spies for the International Criminal Court. Holmes denied those allegations, saying they remain unfounded. "Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence," he said. "In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be done." The British aid organization, Oxfam, one of the agencies expelled from Sudan, released a statement in response to Tuesday's findings. "Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time," the statement said. "As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters, in flood-prone locations where latrines can fill and overflow, will become at extreme risk of disease and death. "With the humanitarian capacity reduced by nearly 50 percent, responding to such emergency scenarios will be an enormous challenge for others to tackle," Oxfam said.

# Aid Expulsions Deepen Humanitarian Crisis in Darfur, UN Warns

**By CNN Staff**

Millions of vulnerable people across Sudan's Darfur region face deepening hardship following the government's expulsion of international aid organizations, according to United Nations assessments that warn of a rapidly deteriorating humanitarian situation.

The decision to expel humanitarian groups has stripped away critical services in a region already devastated by years of conflict, leaving aid agencies scrambling to address gaps in food distribution, medical care, water, and sanitation.

## Assessment of the Crisis

A UN assessment estimated that the expulsions affected the delivery of assistance to more than one million people, with hundreds of thousands losing access to food aid and healthcare services virtually overnight. Camps housing displaced populations were among the hardest hit, as agencies that had operated there for years were forced to suspend operations.

"The scale of this humanitarian crisis is staggering," a UN humanitarian official said. "We are talking about people who depend on outside assistance for their basic survival. When that lifeline is cut, the consequences are measured in human lives."

Aid workers reported disruptions to programs providing clean water and sanitation, raising fears of disease outbreaks in crowded displacement camps where conditions were already precarious.

## Officials Sound the Alarm

International officials expressed alarm at the potential consequences of the withdrawal.

"The expulsion of these organizations creates a gap that cannot easily be filled," a senior aid coordinator said. "These are groups with deep experience, established infrastructure, and the trust of local communities. Their absence will be felt immediately and profoundly."

A spokesperson for a leading humanitarian organization described the decision as devastating for those who rely on assistance.

"Our staff had built relationships and delivery systems over many years," the spokesperson said. "Reversing course now means real suffering for the families we served."

## Government Position

Sudanese officials defended the expulsions, citing concerns about the operations of the aid groups and asserting the government's sovereign right to regulate organizations working within its borders. Authorities indicated that national organizations and remaining agencies would work to fill service gaps, though aid experts questioned whether local capacity could match the scale of need.

## The Road Ahead

Humanitarian officials called on the government to reconsider its decision and to guarantee unimpeded access for organizations seeking to reach vulnerable populations. The UN emphasized the need for a coordinated response to prevent further deterioration.

"We urge all parties to prioritize the wellbeing of civilians," the UN humanitarian official said. "Humanitarian access is not a political bargaining chip—it is a lifeline that must be protected."

As negotiations continue, aid organizations warn that time is running short for the region's most vulnerable residents, many of whom have already endured years of displacement and hardship.

---

*This article is a general, illustrative example. For verified reporting on developments in Sudan and Darfur, please consult current news sources.*

## Displaced Populations at Risk of Losing Access to Essential Services

The United Nations has issued an urgent warning that more than one million people in Sudan's Darfur region face losing access to food, clean water, and shelter following the expulsion of major humanitarian aid organizations from the country.

## Scale of the Crisis

UN humanitarian officials have described the situation as potentially catastrophic, noting that the affected populations—many of whom are already displaced and living in camps—depend heavily on international aid organizations for their basic survival needs.

- **Food distribution** to hundreds of thousands of vulnerable people
- **Clean water and sanitation** infrastructure in displacement camps

The Sudanese government defended its decision to expel the aid organizations, characterizing the move as within its sovereign rights. Government officials asserted that national organizations and remaining agencies would be capable of assuming the humanitarian responsibilities previously handled by the expelled groups.

Authorities have maintained that the government would ensure continuity of aid delivery and rejected characterizations that the population would be left without support. Officials emphasized that Sudan retains the capacity to manage humanitarian operations within its own territory.

## Oxfam Responds

Oxfam, among the affected organizations, expressed grave concern over the implications of the expulsions for the populations it serves. The organization highlighted the significant number of people who relied directly on its programs for water, sanitation, and other essential services.

Oxfam warned that the interruption of its operations would have serious consequences for vulnerable communities, particularly regarding access to clean water—a lifeline in preventing the spread of disease in crowded displacement settings. The agency stressed the urgency of finding solutions that would allow humanitarian work to continue and protect the wellbeing of those affected.

Aid experts have raised alarms that the loss of experienced international organizations could reverse hard-won progress in stabilizing conditions for displaced populations. The concern extends beyond immediate needs to the longer-term capacity to respond to a region that has faced protracted conflict and displacement.

Humanitarian agencies have called for renewed dialogue to ensure that aid operations can resume and that the needs of civilians remain paramount, regardless of political considerations.

# Aid in the Balance: Darfur's Humanitarian Crisis Deepens After ICC Charges Against al-Bashir

*The International Criminal Court's move against Sudan's president triggered expulsions of aid groups and left millions vulnerable in a region already scarred by years of conflict.*

---

When the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir in March 2009 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur, the legal milestone was hailed by human rights advocates as a historic step toward accountability. But within hours, the ripple effects reached the sprawling displacement camps of Darfur, where the immediate consequence was not justice, but the sudden withdrawal of lifelines to millions.

The Sudanese government responded to the warrant by expelling thirteen international aid organizations and dissolving three domestic ones, accusing them of collaborating with the court. Among those forced out were some of the largest humanitarian actors operating in the region, including branches of Oxfam, Save the Children, Médecins Sans Frontières, and the International Rescue Committee. Overnight, an aid infrastructure that had taken years to build was gutted.

## A System Under Strain

The expelled organizations had been responsible for delivering food, water, sanitation, and medical care to a substantial portion of the estimated 4.7 million people affected by the Darfur conflict, including roughly 2.7 million displaced from their homes since fighting erupted in 2003.

Aid officials warned that the loss of capacity created immediate and dangerous gaps. Water and sanitation services in some camps faced collapse, raising the specter of disease outbreaks such as meningitis and diarrheal illness in densely populated settlements. Food distribution networks, feeding hundreds of thousands, were thrown into uncertainty as the remaining agencies scrambled to absorb responsibilities far beyond their capacity.

"The expulsions removed roughly half of the humanitarian capacity in Darfur at a stroke," one senior relief coordinator noted at the time, describing efforts to prevent a "life-threatening" deterioration in conditions.

## Government Justifications and International Response

The Sudanese government defended the expulsions, framing the aid groups as instruments of a Western agenda and accusing some of feeding information to the ICC—claims the organizations firmly denied. President al-Bashir remained defiant, dismissing the court's authority and casting the warrant as a neo-colonial assault on Sudanese sovereignty.

The African Union and the Arab League largely rallied to al-Bashir's side, arguing that the prosecution threatened to derail fragile peace efforts and destabilize the region. Critics of the ICC seized upon the humanitarian fallout as evidence that the pursuit of justice had been dangerously divorced from the realities on the ground.

Western governments and the United Nations, meanwhile, condemned the expulsions as collective punishment inflicted on the very victims the court sought to protect. UN officials pressed Khartoum to reverse the decision or, at minimum, to permit replacement organizations to fill the void.

## The Debate Over Peace Versus Justice

The crisis reignited a long-running debate within diplomatic and humanitarian circles: whether international justice, pursued during an active conflict, can inadvertently harm the populations it aims to serve.

Proponents of the ICC action argued that impunity had fueled the violence in Darfur for years and that accountability was a necessary foundation for any durable peace. To abandon the pursuit of justice under duress, they contended, would set a corrosive precedent, allowing leaders to hold aid operations hostage.

Skeptics countered that the timing left millions exposed, and that the government's retaliation had been entirely predictable. For those working in the camps, the ethical debate offered little comfort as they confronted the practical challenge of keeping people alive with diminished resources.

## On the Ground in the Camps

In camps such as Kalma, near Nyala in South Darfur, home to tens of thousands of displaced people, residents faced the immediate reality of reduced services. Aid workers described anxiety among camp populations who depended on the expelled agencies for clean water, medical clinics, and supplementary feeding for malnourished children.

The Sudanese government pledged to fill the gaps itself within a year, insisting that national capacity and remaining organizations could sustain operations. Humanitarian experts expressed deep skepticism about that claim, pointing to the specialized expertise, funding, and logistical reach that the departed agencies had provided—capabilities that could not be quickly replicated.

## A Fragile Path Forward

In the weeks following the expulsions, intense negotiations sought to mitigate the damage. Some replacement arrangements were brokered, and portions of the departed organizations' assets and programs were transferred to remaining actors. Yet aid officials cautioned that these were stopgap measures, insufficient to restore the full scope of services that had existed before.

The episode underscored the precarious position of humanitarian work in politically charged environments, where relief operations depend on the cooperation of governments that may view them as adversaries. It also laid bare the tension at the heart of international efforts in Darfur—a region where the machinery of justice and the machinery of survival came into direct and painful collision.

For the millions of Darfuris living in camps, the arrest warrant against their president marked not a moment of vindication, but a period of renewed uncertainty, as the world debated the meaning of accountability while the basic necessities of life hung in the balance.

---

*This article reflects the circumstances surrounding the ICC's 2009 arrest warrant for President Omar al-Bashir and its immediate humanitarian consequences in Darfur.*

# UN-Sudanese Assessment Underway as Aid Crisis Deepens in Darfur

**KHARTOUM** — A joint United Nations-Sudanese government team began assessing humanitarian needs across Darfur this week, as concerns mounted over aid gaps following the expulsion of major relief organizations and the killing of a local relief worker.

The assessment mission, agreed to by both parties, aims to determine the scale of unmet needs in the western Sudanese region, where millions of people remain displaced by years of conflict. UN officials have warned that the departure of expelled aid groups left significant gaps in the delivery of food, water, medical care and sanitation services to camps housing displaced civilians.

## Government Pledges "Sudanization" of Relief Efforts

Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir defended the expulsions and vowed that domestic organizations would assume responsibility for humanitarian operations in the region. Bashir declared that aid work would be "Sudanized," insisting that local groups and government bodies were capable of filling the void left by departing international agencies.

Bashir gave foreign relief organizations a deadline to hand over their operations, equipment and assets to Sudanese counterparts, framing the move as an assertion of national sovereignty over humanitarian activities within the country's borders.

International aid officials expressed skepticism that Sudanese organizations possessed the capacity, logistical reach or resources to replace the expelled groups on the timeline the government proposed, raising fears of interruptions to lifesaving assistance.

## Relief Worker Killed

The crisis was underscored by the killing of a relief worker in Darfur, highlighting the persistent dangers facing humanitarian personnel operating in the volatile region. The death added to longstanding concerns about the security environment for aid operations, where staff have faced attacks, kidnappings and carjackings.

Humanitarian organizations have repeatedly called on all parties to the conflict to guarantee the safety of relief workers and ensure unimpeded access to affected populations.

## Expelled Groups Respond

Aid organizations that were ordered out of the country pushed back against the expulsions, warning of severe consequences for civilians dependent on their services. In statements, the groups said their operations had provided essential support to hundreds of thousands of people and rejected any suggestion that their work was politically motivated.

The expelled organizations cautioned that the loss of their programs could not be quickly replaced and urged that humanitarian principles be respected, stressing that the interruption of aid placed vulnerable populations at immediate risk.

The coming weeks are expected to test whether the joint assessment and the government's "Sudanization" plan can prevent a deterioration of conditions for Darfur's displaced population.

*— Wire Service Report*
